CHAPTER 11 - PERMUTATIONS AND COMBINATIONS

Introduction

In everyday life we often need to count the number of ways in which a task can be done: the number of different telephone numbers, the number of ways a committee can be chosen, the number of arrangements of letters in a word, the number of routes between two towns. When the number of possibilities is small we can list them all, but when it is large this becomes impractical. Permutations and combinations give us quick, systematic methods of counting WITHOUT actually listing every case. This chapter builds these methods from a single idea - the fundamental principle of counting - and then develops factorial notation, permutations (arrangements) and combinations (selections), together with their properties and many applications.

11.1 THE FUNDAMENTAL PRINCIPLE OF COUNTING

MULTIPLICATION PRINCIPLE. If one event can occur in m different ways and, following it, a second event can occur in n different ways, then the two events can occur together (in succession) in m x n different ways. More generally, if a task is completed in several stages and stage 1 can be done in n1 ways, stage 2 in n2 ways, ..., stage k in nk ways, then the whole task can be done in n1 x n2 x ... x nk ways. The key word is AND - when we do one thing AND then another, we MULTIPLY.

Example: A boy has 3 shirts and 4 trousers. He can dress in 3 x 4 = 12 different ways, because for each of the 3 shirts there are 4 choices of trousers.

Example: How many two-digit numbers can be formed from the digits 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 if repetition is allowed? The tens place can be filled in 5 ways and the units place in 5 ways, so 5 x 5 = 25 numbers. If repetition is NOT allowed, the tens place has 5 choices and the units place then has 4 choices, giving 5 x 4 = 20.

ADDITION PRINCIPLE. If one event can occur in m ways and another, mutually exclusive, event can occur in n ways, then one OR the other can occur in m + n ways. The key word is OR (with no overlap) - we ADD.

Example: A student can travel from town A to town B by 3 bus routes or 2 train routes. The number of ways of travelling from A to B is 3 + 2 = 5 (choose a bus OR a train). But if the student goes A to B and then B to C (3 ways A-B, 2 ways B-C), the number of ways for the whole journey is 3 x 2 = 6, because now both stages must be done.

11.2 FACTORIAL NOTATION

The product of the first n natural numbers is written n! (read 'n factorial'):

   n! = n x (n - 1) x (n - 2) x ... x 3 x 2 x 1.

Thus 1! = 1, 2! = 2, 3! = 6, 4! = 24, 5! = 120, 6! = 720. By convention 0! = 1; this makes the later formulas work smoothly. A very useful property is the recursion n! = n x (n - 1)!, for example 7! = 7 x 6!. Factorials grow extremely fast.

Example: Evaluate 8! / 6!. Writing 8! = 8 x 7 x 6!, we get 8! / 6! = 8 x 7 = 56. We rarely expand large factorials in full - instead we cancel common factors. Similarly (n + 1)! / (n - 1)! = (n + 1) x n.

Example: Find n if n! = 12 x (n - 2)!. Since n! = n x (n - 1) x (n - 2)!, we need n(n - 1) = 12, i.e. n^2 - n - 12 = 0, (n - 4)(n + 3) = 0, so n = 4 (rejecting the negative value).

11.3 PERMUTATIONS OF DISTINCT OBJECTS

A PERMUTATION is an ARRANGEMENT of objects in a definite ORDER. Order matters: the arrangement AB is different from BA. The number of permutations of n distinct objects taken r at a time is written nPr (also P(n, r)). To fill r places in order from n distinct objects, the first place can be filled in n ways, the second in (n - 1) ways, the third in (n - 2) ways, and so on down to the r-th place in (n - r + 1) ways. By the multiplication principle,

   nPr = n (n - 1)(n - 2) ... (n - r + 1).

Multiplying and dividing by (n - r)! gives the compact factorial form

   nPr = n! / (n - r)!,   where 0 <= r <= n.

Two special cases: nPn = n! (all n objects arranged among themselves) and nP0 = 1. Also nP1 = n.

Example: In how many ways can 3 letters be chosen and arranged from the 5 letters A, B, C, D, E? This is 5P3 = 5! / 2! = 5 x 4 x 3 = 60.

Example: How many different 4-digit numbers can be formed from the digits 1-9 (no repetition)? We arrange 4 of the 9 distinct digits: 9P4 = 9 x 8 x 7 x 6 = 3024.

Example: In how many ways can 6 students be seated in a row? This is 6P6 = 6! = 720.

11.4 PERMUTATIONS WITH REPETITION AND WITH ALIKE OBJECTS

PERMUTATIONS WITH REPETITION ALLOWED. If any of the n objects may be used again and again, then each of the r places can be filled in n ways, so the number of arrangements is n^r (n raised to the power r). For example, the number of 3-letter code words using the 26 letters of the alphabet, with repetition allowed, is 26^3 = 17576. The number of ways of posting 5 letters into 3 letter-boxes is 3^5 = 243 (each letter chooses one of 3 boxes).

PERMUTATIONS OF OBJECTS THAT ARE NOT ALL DISTINCT. If, out of n objects, p are alike of one kind, q are alike of a second kind and r are alike of a third kind (and the rest are distinct), then the number of distinct arrangements of all n objects is

   n! / (p! q! r!).

We divide by the factorials because permuting the identical objects among themselves does not create a new arrangement.

Example: How many arrangements can be made of the letters of the word MISSISSIPPI? There are 11 letters: M(1), I(4), S(4), P(2). The number of arrangements is 11! / (1! 4! 4! 2!) = 39916800 / (24 x 24 x 2) = 34650.

Example: The number of arrangements of the letters of the word BANANA (6 letters: B(1), A(3), N(2)) is 6! / (3! 2!) = 720 / 12 = 60.

CIRCULAR PERMUTATIONS. When objects are arranged in a CIRCLE (round a table, on a ring), there is no fixed first position - only relative order matters. Fixing one object to remove the rotational duplication, the remaining (n - 1) objects can be arranged in (n - 1)! ways. Hence the number of circular arrangements of n distinct objects is (n - 1)!. For example, 5 people can sit around a round table in (5 - 1)! = 4! = 24 ways. If, in addition, clockwise and anticlockwise arrangements are regarded as the SAME (as for a garland of flowers or a necklace of beads), the number is (n - 1)! / 2.

11.5 COMBINATIONS

A COMBINATION is a SELECTION of objects in which ORDER does NOT matter. The selection {A, B} is the same as {B, A}. The number of combinations of n distinct objects taken r at a time is written nCr (also C(n, r) or the binomial coefficient). Each selection of r objects can itself be arranged in r! orders, and those r! arrangements are all counted separately in nPr but only once in nCr. Therefore nPr = r! x nCr, which gives

   nCr = nPr / r! = n! / (r! (n - r)!),   0 <= r <= n.

The relation nPr = r! nCr is worth remembering: permutations = selections then arrangements. Special values: nC0 = 1, nCn = 1, nC1 = n.

Example: In how many ways can a committee of 3 be chosen from 8 people? Order does not matter, so we use 8C3 = 8! / (3! 5!) = (8 x 7 x 6) / (3 x 2 x 1) = 56.

Example: From a pack of 52 cards, how many ways are there to choose 5 cards? 52C5 = 2598960.

Example: A bag has 5 red and 4 blue balls. In how many ways can 3 balls be chosen so that 2 are red and 1 is blue? Choose 2 red from 5 (5C2 = 10) AND 1 blue from 4 (4C1 = 4), giving 10 x 4 = 40.

11.6 DIFFERENCE BETWEEN PERMUTATION AND COMBINATION

A permutation is an ARRANGEMENT (order matters); a combination is a SELECTION (order does not matter). Whenever a problem involves the words 'arrange', 'seat in a row', 'form a number', 'ranking' or 'schedule', order matters and we use permutations. Whenever it involves 'select', 'choose', 'committee', 'group', 'team' or 'draw', order does not matter and we use combinations. Since each selection of r objects can be arranged in r! ways, always nPr = r! x nCr, so nPr is r! times larger than nCr (for r >= 2).

11.7 PROPERTIES OF nCr

(i) SYMMETRY: nCr = nC(n - r). Choosing r objects to keep is the same as choosing the (n - r) objects to leave out. For example 10C7 = 10C3 = 120.

(ii) PASCAL'S RULE: nCr + nC(r - 1) = (n + 1)Cr. This identity underlies Pascal's triangle, in which each entry is the sum of the two entries above it.

(iii) If nCx = nCy then either x = y or x + y = n. This follows from the symmetry property and is often used to find an unknown.

(iv) The sum of all the combinations nC0 + nC1 + nC2 + ... + nCn = 2^n, which is the total number of subsets (including the empty set) of a set of n elements.

Example: If nC8 = nC12, find n. By the property, 8 + 12 = n, so n = 20 (since 8 is not equal to 12). Then nC2 = 20C2 = 190.

Example: Verify Pascal's rule with n = 5, r = 2: 5C2 + 5C1 = 10 + 5 = 15 = 6C2. Correct.

11.8 APPLICATIONS AND WORD PROBLEMS

COMMITTEE PROBLEMS. From 7 men and 4 women, in how many ways can a committee of 5 be formed containing exactly 3 men and 2 women? Choose 3 men from 7 (7C3 = 35) AND 2 women from 4 (4C2 = 6): 35 x 6 = 210.

'AT LEAST' PROBLEMS. From 7 men and 4 women, a committee of 5 with AT LEAST 3 women means (3 women, 2 men) OR (4 women, 1 man): (4C3 x 7C2) + (4C4 x 7C1) = (4 x 21) + (1 x 7) = 84 + 7 = 91.

ARRANGEMENT WITH A CONDITION. In how many ways can the letters of the word DELHI be arranged so that the vowels (E, I) are always together? Treat the two vowels as one block: we then arrange 4 items (the block and D, L, H) in 4! = 24 ways, and the 2 vowels within the block in 2! = 2 ways, giving 24 x 2 = 48 arrangements.

GEOMETRY APPLICATIONS. How many straight lines can be drawn through 10 points, no three of which are collinear? A line needs 2 points, and order does not matter, so 10C2 = 45. How many triangles? A triangle needs 3 non-collinear points, so 10C3 = 120. How many diagonals has a polygon of n sides? Join any 2 of the n vertices (nC2) and subtract the n sides: nC2 - n = n(n - 3)/2. For a hexagon (n = 6) this is 6 x 3 / 2 = 9.

HANDSHAKE PROBLEM. If every pair of people in a room of 12 shakes hands once, the number of handshakes is 12C2 = 66 (a handshake is an unordered pair).

SUMMARY

- Fundamental principle of counting: for tasks in stages, MULTIPLY the number of ways (AND); for mutually exclusive alternatives, ADD the number of ways (OR).
- Factorial: n! = n(n - 1)(n - 2)...2 x 1, with 0! = 1 and n! = n x (n - 1)!.
- Permutation = arrangement (order matters): nPr = n! / (n - r)!, nPn = n!, nP0 = 1.
- With repetition allowed, arrangements of r places from n objects = n^r.
- With p, q, r alike objects among n, distinct arrangements = n! / (p! q! r!).
- Circular permutations of n distinct objects = (n - 1)!; if reflections are the same, (n - 1)! / 2.
- Combination = selection (order does not matter): nCr = n! / (r!(n - r)!), and nPr = r! x nCr.
- Properties: nCr = nC(n - r); nCr + nC(r - 1) = (n + 1)Cr; if nCx = nCy then x = y or x + y = n; sum of nCr over r = 2^n.
- Applications: committees and selections use combinations; arrangements and numbers use permutations; geometry (lines nC2, triangles nC3, diagonals nC2 - n) and handshakes use combinations.

topics.name: Fundamental Principle of Counting
topics.description: The multiplication principle (do this AND that: multiply n1 x n2 x ... ways) and the addition principle (do this OR that, mutually exclusive: add m + n ways), with counting of numbers, routes and arrangements.

topics.name: Factorial Notation
topics.description: The factorial n! = n(n-1)(n-2)...2x1, the convention 0! = 1, the recursion n! = n x (n-1)!, evaluating and simplifying factorial expressions such as n!/(n-r)! by cancelling common factors.

topics.name: Permutations of Distinct Objects
topics.description: Arrangements in which order matters; nPr = n(n-1)...(n-r+1) = n!/(n-r)! for n distinct objects taken r at a time; special cases nPn = n!, nP0 = 1, nP1 = n.

topics.name: Permutations with Repetition and Alike Objects
topics.description: Arrangements of r places from n objects when repetition is allowed (n^r); permutations of n objects when some are alike, n!/(p! q! r!); and circular permutations (n-1)! or (n-1)!/2 for necklaces.

topics.name: Combinations
topics.description: Selections in which order does not matter; nCr = n!/(r!(n-r)!); the relation nPr = r! x nCr; special values nC0 = nCn = 1, nC1 = n; and the difference between permutations and combinations.

topics.name: Properties of Combinations and Applications
topics.description: Properties nCr = nC(n-r), Pascal's rule nCr + nC(r-1) = (n+1)Cr, the rule nCx = nCy implies x = y or x + y = n, and applications to committees, selections, geometry (lines, triangles, diagonals) and handshakes.

learning_outcomes.description: State and apply the multiplication and addition principles of counting to find the number of ways of performing tasks that occur in stages or as mutually exclusive alternatives.
Define factorial notation n!, use the convention 0! = 1 and the recursion n! = n x (n-1)!, and evaluate or simplify expressions involving factorials by cancelling common factors.
Explain the meaning of a permutation as an ordered arrangement and derive the formula nPr = n!/(n-r)! for permutations of n distinct objects taken r at a time.
Apply nPr = n!/(n-r)! to count arrangements of distinct objects, form numbers from digits without repetition, and solve seating and word-arrangement problems.

learning_outcomes.topic_name: Permutations with Repetition and Alike Objects
learning_outcomes.description: Count arrangements when repetition is allowed (n^r), when some objects are alike (n!/(p! q! r!)), and around a circle ((n-1)! or (n-1)!/2).
Explain a combination as an unordered selection, derive nCr = n!/(r!(n-r)!) using nPr = r! x nCr, and distinguish permutations from combinations.
Apply nCr to select objects, form committees or teams, and solve grouping problems including selections drawn from two or more categories.
Use and analyse the properties nCr = nC(n-r), Pascal's rule and nCx = nCy, and apply combinations to geometry (lines, triangles, diagonals), handshakes and 'at least' problems.

chapter_summary.title: Permutations and Combinations - Chapter Summary
chapter_summary.intro: This NIOS Senior Secondary Mathematics summary develops systematic counting: the fundamental principle of counting, factorial notation, permutations (ordered arrangements), permutations with repetition and alike objects, combinations (unordered selections), the properties of nCr, and their many applications to committees, numbers, geometry and handshakes.

branches.label: Properties & Uses
details: Lines nC2, triangles nC3, diagonals nC2 - n

sections.heading: Fundamental principle of counting
bullets: Multiplication principle: if a task is done in stages with n1, n2, ..., nk ways, the whole task has n1 x n2 x ... x nk ways (the word AND means multiply).
Addition principle: mutually exclusive alternatives with m and n ways give m + n ways (the word OR, with no overlap, means add).
Example: 3 shirts and 4 trousers give 3 x 4 = 12 outfits; two-digit numbers from 1-5 without repetition give 5 x 4 = 20.

sections.heading: Factorial notation
bullets: n! = n(n-1)(n-2)...2 x 1 is the product of the first n natural numbers; it grows very fast.
By convention 0! = 1, and the recursion n! = n x (n-1)! lets us cancel, e.g. 8!/6! = 8 x 7 = 56.
Factorials appear in every permutation and combination formula.

sections.heading: Permutations
bullets: A permutation is an arrangement where ORDER matters; nPr = n!/(n-r)! = n(n-1)...(n-r+1).
Special cases: nPn = n!, nP0 = 1, nP1 = n; e.g. 5P3 = 60, 6P6 = 720.
With repetition allowed, r places from n objects give n^r; with p, q, r alike objects, arrangements are n!/(p! q! r!).
Circular permutations of n distinct objects are (n-1)!, and (n-1)!/2 when reflections (necklaces) coincide.

sections.heading: Combinations
bullets: A combination is a selection where ORDER does not matter; nCr = n!/(r!(n-r)!).
Since each selection can be arranged in r! ways, nPr = r! x nCr, so nPr is r! times nCr.
Special values nC0 = nCn = 1, nC1 = n; e.g. a committee of 3 from 8 is 8C3 = 56.

sections.heading: Properties of nCr and applications
bullets: Symmetry nCr = nC(n-r); Pascal's rule nCr + nC(r-1) = (n+1)Cr; if nCx = nCy then x = y or x + y = n.
Sum nC0 + nC1 + ... + nCn = 2^n is the number of subsets of an n-element set.
Geometry: through n points (no 3 collinear) there are nC2 lines and nC3 triangles; a polygon of n sides has nC2 - n = n(n-3)/2 diagonals.
'At least' problems are split into exclusive cases and added, e.g. at least 3 women = (3W,2M) + (4W,1M).

key_takeaways: Multiplication principle (AND) multiplies stage counts; addition principle (OR, exclusive) adds them.
n! = n(n-1)...2 x 1 with 0! = 1; simplify factorials by cancelling, e.g. 8!/6! = 56.
Permutations count ordered arrangements: nPr = n!/(n-r)!; nPn = n!.
Repetition gives n^r; alike objects give n!/(p! q! r!); circular arrangements give (n-1)!.
Combinations count unordered selections: nCr = n!/(r!(n-r)!), with nPr = r! x nCr.
Key properties: nCr = nC(n-r) and nCr + nC(r-1) = (n+1)Cr; nCx = nCy implies x = y or x + y = n.
Applications: committees and teams use nCr; arrangements and numbers use nPr; lines nC2, triangles nC3, diagonals nC2 - n.

glossary.definition: The rule that tasks done in stages multiply their number of ways (AND), while mutually exclusive alternatives add (OR).
If stages have n1, n2, ..., nk ways, the whole task can be done in n1 x n2 x ... x nk ways.
If two mutually exclusive events have m and n ways, then one or the other can happen in m + n ways.
The product of the first n natural numbers, n! = n(n-1)(n-2)...2 x 1, with 0! defined as 1.
An arrangement of objects in a definite order; the number of n distinct objects taken r at a time is nPr = n!/(n-r)!.
The number of permutations of n distinct objects taken r at a time, nPr = n!/(n-r)! = n(n-1)...(n-r+1).
Filling r ordered places from n objects when each may repeat, giving n^r arrangements.
Arrangements of n objects of which p, q, r are alike, equal to n!/(p! q! r!).
An arrangement of n distinct objects around a circle, equal to (n-1)!, or (n-1)!/2 when reflections coincide.
A selection of objects in which order does not matter; nCr = n!/(r!(n-r)!).
The number of combinations of n distinct objects taken r at a time, nCr = n!/(r!(n-r)!) = nPr/r!.
nCr = nC(n-r): choosing r to keep is the same as choosing (n-r) to reject.
The identity nCr + nC(r-1) = (n+1)Cr, which generates Pascal's triangle.
The number of diagonals of a polygon of n sides is nC2 - n = n(n-3)/2.
The number of handshakes among n people, each pair once, is nC2 = n(n-1)/2.

worksheet.title: Worksheet - Permutations and Combinations (NIOS Senior Secondary Mathematics)
worksheet.instructions: Attempt all questions. Show full working for numerical problems. Take 0! = 1 and leave answers as exact integers unless asked otherwise.

questions.question: State the multiplication and addition principles of counting, giving one short example of each.
questions.answer:
Multiplication principle: if a task is done in successive stages that can occur in n1, n2, ..., nk ways, the whole task can be done in n1 x n2 x ... x nk ways (used when we do one stage AND another). Example: with 3 shirts and 4 trousers, the number of outfits is 3 x 4 = 12.

Addition principle: if two events are mutually exclusive and can occur in m and n ways, then one OR the other can occur in m + n ways. Example: travelling A to B by 3 bus routes or 2 train routes gives 3 + 2 = 5 ways.
questions.explanation: AND -> multiply; OR (exclusive) -> add, with an example each.

questions.question: Evaluate 10! / (7! 3!) showing the cancellation.
Find n if nP2 = 20.
questions.answer: nP2 = n(n - 1) = 20, so n^2 - n - 20 = 0. Factorising: (n - 5)(n + 4) = 0, giving n = 5 or n = -4. Since n must be a positive integer, n = 5.
questions.explanation: nP2 = n(n-1); solve the quadratic, reject negative root.

questions.question: How many 4-digit numbers can be formed using the digits 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7 if no digit is repeated?
questions.answer:
We arrange 4 of the 7 distinct digits in order, so the count is 7P4 = 7 x 6 x 5 x 4 = 840.

Hence 840 four-digit numbers can be formed.

questions.question: How many different arrangements can be made using all the letters of the word MATHEMATICS?
questions.answer:
MATHEMATICS has 11 letters: M(2), A(2), T(2), H(1), E(1), I(1), C(1), S(1). With three pairs of alike letters,

   arrangements = 11! / (2! 2! 2!) = 39916800 / 8 = 4989600.

So 4989600 distinct arrangements are possible.
questions.explanation: n!/(p! q! r!) with M, A, T each twice: 11!/(2!2!2!).

questions.question: Prove that nPr = r! x nCr, and hence write nCr in factorial form.
questions.answer:
Each selection (combination) of r objects from n can itself be arranged among the r places in r! different orders. Every one of these r! orders is a distinct permutation, and every permutation of r objects arises this way exactly once. Therefore the number of permutations equals the number of combinations multiplied by r!:

   nPr = r! x nCr.

Since nPr = n!/(n - r)!, dividing by r! gives

   nCr = nPr / r! = n! / (r! (n - r)!).
questions.explanation: Each combination gives r! permutations; divide nPr by r!.

questions.question: A committee of 5 is to be formed from 7 men and 4 women. In how many ways can this be done if the committee must contain (a) exactly 3 men and 2 women, (b) at least 3 women?
questions.answer:
(a) Exactly 3 men and 2 women: choose 3 men from 7 AND 2 women from 4.
   7C3 = (7 x 6 x 5)/(3 x 2 x 1) = 35, and 4C2 = (4 x 3)/(2 x 1) = 6.
   Number of committees = 35 x 6 = 210.

(b) At least 3 women means (3 women and 2 men) OR (4 women and 1 man), which are mutually exclusive, so add:
   Case 3W, 2M: 4C3 x 7C2 = 4 x 21 = 84.
   Case 4W, 1M: 4C4 x 7C1 = 1 x 7 = 7.
   Total = 84 + 7 = 91.

So (a) 210 committees and (b) 91 committees.
questions.explanation: Multiply within a case (AND), add across exclusive cases (OR).

questions.question: If nC8 = nC12, find the value of n and hence evaluate nC2.
questions.answer:
Using the property nCx = nCy implies x = y or x + y = n. Here 8 is not equal to 12, so x + y = n gives n = 8 + 12 = 20.

Then nC2 = 20C2 = (20 x 19)/(2 x 1) = 190.
questions.explanation: nCx = nCy with x != y gives n = x + y = 20; 20C2 = 190.

questions.question: There are 12 points in a plane, no three of which are collinear. How many straight lines and how many triangles can be formed by joining them?
questions.answer:
A straight line is fixed by any 2 of the points, and order does not matter, so the number of lines = 12C2 = (12 x 11)/2 = 66.

A triangle is fixed by any 3 non-collinear points, so the number of triangles = 12C3 = (12 x 11 x 10)/(3 x 2 x 1) = 220.

Hence 66 lines and 220 triangles.

questions.question: In how many ways can the letters of the word DAUGHTER be arranged so that (a) all the vowels occur together, (b) the arrangement begins with D and ends with R?
questions.answer:
DAUGHTER has 8 distinct letters, with 3 vowels (A, U, E) and 5 consonants (D, G, H, T, R).

(a) Vowels together: treat the 3 vowels as a single block. Then we arrange 6 items (the block plus D, G, H, T, R) in 6! = 720 ways, and the 3 vowels within the block in 3! = 6 ways. Total = 6! x 3! = 720 x 6 = 4320.

(b) Begins with D and ends with R: fix D in the first place and R in the last place. The remaining 6 letters (A, U, G, H, T, E) fill the 6 middle places in 6! = 720 ways. Total = 720.
questions.explanation: (a) block of vowels: 6! x 3! = 4320; (b) fix D and R, arrange 6 middle letters: 6! = 720.

questions.question: If nC3 = nC5, then n = ______.
The number of triangles formed by 6 points, no 3 collinear, is ______.
How many 3-digit numbers can be formed using the digits 0-9 if repetition is not allowed?
questions.answer:
The hundreds place cannot be 0, so it has 9 choices (1-9). The tens place can be any of the remaining 9 digits (0 now allowed), and the units place any of the remaining 8 digits.

   Total = 9 x 9 x 8 = 648.

questions.question: Explain, with the shirt-trouser example, the difference between using AND (multiply) and OR (add).
questions.answer:
AND (multiply): choosing a shirt AND a trouser are two stages that must both be done. With 3 shirts and 4 trousers there are 3 x 4 = 12 outfits.

OR (add): if instead you must pick a single item that is EITHER one of 3 shirts OR one of 4 trousers (mutually exclusive), there are 3 + 4 = 7 choices. So AND multiplies stages, OR adds exclusive alternatives.
questions.explanation: AND -> multiply stages; OR -> add exclusive options.

questions.question: How many numbers between 100 and 1000 have all distinct digits (using 0-9)?
questions.answer:
Numbers from 100 to 999 are 3-digit numbers. The hundreds digit has 9 choices (1-9, not 0). The tens digit can be any of the remaining 9 digits (0 allowed). The units digit can be any of the remaining 8 digits.

   Total = 9 x 9 x 8 = 648.
questions.explanation: 3-digit numbers with distinct digits: 9 x 9 x 8 = 648.

questions.question: Simplify (n+2)! / n!.
Find n if (n+1)! = 12 x (n-1)!.
questions.answer:
(n+1)! = (n+1) x n x (n-1)!. Dividing both sides by (n-1)!:

   (n+1) x n = 12

   n^2 + n - 12 = 0, (n + 4)(n - 3) = 0.

So n = 3 (rejecting n = -4).

questions.question: Express 12 x 11 x 10 as a ratio of two factorials.
Derive nPr = n!/(n-r)! using the multiplication principle.
questions.answer:
To arrange r objects in order from n distinct objects, fill r places one by one. The first place has n choices, the second (n-1), the third (n-2), and the r-th place (n-r+1) choices. By the multiplication principle,

   nPr = n(n-1)(n-2)...(n-r+1).

Multiplying and dividing by (n-r)! gives nPr = n!/(n-r)!.

questions.question: In how many ways can the letters of the word EQUATION be arranged? All letters are distinct.
questions.answer:
EQUATION has 8 distinct letters (E, Q, U, A, T, I, O, N). The number of arrangements of 8 distinct letters is

   8! = 40320.

questions.question: How many 4-digit even numbers can be formed from 1,2,3,4,5 without repetition?
questions.answer:
For an even number the units digit must be 2 or 4: 2 choices. The remaining three places are filled from the other 4 digits in 4 x 3 x 2 = 24 ways.

   Total = 2 x 24 = 48.
questions.explanation: Units even (2 ways); other 3 places 4P3 = 24; total 48.

questions.question: In how many ways can 7 students be seated in a row if 2 particular students must not sit together?
questions.answer:
Total arrangements of 7 students = 7! = 5040. Arrangements with the 2 particular students together = treat them as a block: 6! x 2! = 720 x 2 = 1440.

Students not together = 5040 - 1440 = 3600.

questions.question: Solve for n: nP2 = 56.
questions.answer: nP2 = n(n-1) = 56, so n^2 - n - 56 = 0. Factorising: (n - 8)(n + 7) = 0, giving n = 8 (rejecting -7).

questions.question: How many arrangements of the letters of the word ALLAHABAD are possible?
questions.answer:
ALLAHABAD has 9 letters: A(4), L(2), H(1), B(1), D(1). With A four times and L twice,

   arrangements = 9!/(4! 2!) = 362880/(24 x 2) = 362880/48 = 7560.

questions.question: In how many ways can the letters of the word ARRANGE be arranged so that the two R's are never together?
questions.answer:
ARRANGE has 7 letters: A(2), R(2), N, G, E. Total arrangements = 7!/(2!2!) = 5040/4 = 1260.

Arrangements with the two R's together: treat RR as one block, giving 6 items with A twice: 6!/2! = 720/2 = 360.

R's never together = 1260 - 360 = 900.

questions.question: In how many ways can 5 boys and 3 girls sit around a round table?
questions.answer:
For a circular arrangement of 8 distinct people, fix one person to remove rotational duplication; the rest are arranged in (8-1)! ways.

   Number of ways = 7! = 5040.

questions.question: Evaluate 9C3 and 9C6, and comment on the result.
questions.answer:
9C3 = (9 x 8 x 7)/(3 x 2 x 1) = 504/6 = 84.
9C6 = 9C(9-6) = 9C3 = 84.

They are equal, illustrating the symmetry property nCr = nC(n-r).

questions.question: Explain the difference between 5P3 and 5C3 with their values.
questions.answer:
5C3 is the number of SELECTIONS of 3 objects from 5 (order ignored): 5C3 = 10. 5P3 is the number of ARRANGEMENTS of 3 objects from 5 (order counts): 5P3 = 60.

They are related by 5P3 = 3! x 5C3 = 6 x 10 = 60, because each of the 10 selections can be arranged in 3! = 6 orders.

questions.question: From 8 men and 5 women, how many committees of 4 contain at least 3 men?
questions.answer:
At least 3 men means (3 men, 1 woman) OR (4 men, 0 women):
Case 3M,1W: 8C3 x 5C1 = 56 x 5 = 280.
Case 4M,0W: 8C4 x 5C0 = 70 x 1 = 70.

Total = 280 + 70 = 350.

questions.question: In how many ways can a cricket team of 11 be chosen from 15 players if 2 particular players are always included?
questions.answer:
The 2 particular players are fixed, so we must choose the remaining 11 - 2 = 9 players from the remaining 15 - 2 = 13 players.

   Number of ways = 13C9 = 13C4 = (13 x 12 x 11 x 10)/(4 x 3 x 2 x 1) = 17160/24 = 715.

questions.question: A box has 6 red, 4 white and 5 blue balls. In how many ways can 3 balls be drawn so that all are of different colours?
questions.answer:
Choose 1 red, 1 white and 1 blue (one from each colour, all needed together, so multiply):

   6C1 x 4C1 x 5C1 = 6 x 4 x 5 = 120.
questions.explanation: One of each colour: 6 x 4 x 5 = 120.

questions.question: If nC12 = nC8, find n and hence nC17.
questions.answer:
Since 12 is not equal to 8, the property nCx = nCy gives n = 12 + 8 = 20. Then

   nC17 = 20C17 = 20C3 = (20 x 19 x 18)/(3 x 2 x 1) = 6840/6 = 1140.

questions.question: How many diagonals does a polygon of 10 sides (decagon) have?
questions.answer:
Number of diagonals = nC2 - n = n(n-3)/2 for an n-sided polygon.

   = 10 x 7 / 2 = 70/2 = 35.

So a decagon has 35 diagonals.

questions.question: There are 12 points in a plane of which 4 are collinear. How many straight lines can be drawn?
questions.answer:
If no three were collinear, the number of lines would be 12C2 = 66. But the 4 collinear points, which would give 4C2 = 6 separate lines, actually give only 1 line.

   Lines = 12C2 - 4C2 + 1 = 66 - 6 + 1 = 61.

questions.question: A number-plate consists of 2 distinct letters (A-Z) followed by 3 distinct digits (0-9). How many different plates are possible? Explain each step.
questions.answer:
The plate has 5 positions: 2 letter positions and 3 digit positions.

Letters (distinct): first letter has 26 choices, second has 25 choices: 26 x 25 = 650.
Digits (distinct): first digit has 10 choices, second has 9, third has 8: 10 x 9 x 8 = 720.

By the multiplication principle (letters AND digits), the total number of plates is

   650 x 720 = 468000.

So 468000 different number-plates are possible.

questions.question: (a) Prove the recursion n! = n x (n-1)! from the definition. (b) Hence evaluate 10!/8! and (c) solve n!/(n-2)! = 30.
questions.answer:
(a) By definition n! = n(n-1)(n-2)...2 x 1. The product (n-1)(n-2)...2 x 1 is exactly (n-1)!. Therefore n! = n x (n-1)!.

(b) 10!/8! = (10 x 9 x 8!)/8! = 10 x 9 = 90.

(c) n!/(n-2)! = n(n-1) = 30, so n^2 - n - 30 = 0, (n - 6)(n + 5) = 0, giving n = 6 (rejecting -5).

questions.question: Show that nPr = nP(r-1) x (n - r + 1). Verify the identity for n = 7, r = 3.
questions.answer:
By definition nPr = n!/(n-r)! and nP(r-1) = n!/(n-(r-1))! = n!/(n-r+1)!.

Now (n-r+1)! = (n-r+1) x (n-r)!. So

   nPr / nP(r-1) = [n!/(n-r)!] x [(n-r+1)!/n!] = (n-r+1)!/(n-r)! = (n - r + 1).

Hence nPr = nP(r-1) x (n - r + 1).

Verification (n=7, r=3): 7P3 = 7 x 6 x 5 = 210; 7P2 = 7 x 6 = 42; (n-r+1) = 5. Then 42 x 5 = 210. Verified.

questions.question: In how many ways can the letters of the word ARTICLE be arranged so that (a) the vowels are always together, (b) the vowels occupy only the odd positions?
questions.answer:
ARTICLE has 7 distinct letters: vowels A, I, E (3) and consonants R, T, C, L (4).

(a) Vowels together: treat the 3 vowels as one block. Arrange 5 items (block + 4 consonants) in 5! = 120 ways; arrange the vowels within the block in 3! = 6 ways. Total = 120 x 6 = 720.

(b) Odd positions in a 7-letter word are positions 1, 3, 5, 7 - that is 4 odd places. Place the 3 vowels in 3 of these 4 odd places: 4P3 = 24 ways. The remaining 4 places (one leftover odd place and positions 2, 4, 6) are filled by the 4 consonants: 4! = 24 ways. Total = 24 x 24 = 576.

questions.question: (a) How many arrangements of the word INSTITUTE are possible? (b) In how many of them do all three T's come together?
questions.answer:
INSTITUTE has 9 letters: I(2), N(1), S(1), T(3), U(1), E(1).

(a) Total arrangements = 9!/(2! 3!) = 362880/(2 x 6) = 362880/12 = 30240.

(b) All three T's together: treat TTT as one block. Then we arrange 7 items (the block + I, I, N, S, U, E) where I repeats twice: 7!/2! = 5040/2 = 2520. (The three identical T's inside the block give only 1 internal arrangement.)

So (a) 30240 arrangements and (b) 2520 with the T's together.

questions.question: Define a combination and derive nCr = n!/(r!(n-r)!) from nPr. Hence evaluate the number of ways to choose 4 students from 10 for a quiz team.
questions.answer:
A combination is a selection of objects in which order does not matter; nCr denotes the number of ways of selecting r objects from n distinct objects.

Derivation: each selection of r objects can be arranged among themselves in r! ways, and all these r! ordered arrangements are counted in nPr but represent just ONE combination. Hence nPr = r! x nCr, so

   nCr = nPr / r! = n! / (r!(n-r)!).

Application: choosing 4 students from 10 (order irrelevant) = 10C4 = (10 x 9 x 8 x 7)/(4 x 3 x 2 x 1) = 5040/24 = 210 ways.

questions.question: A question paper has 3 sections A, B, C with 5, 4 and 3 questions respectively. A student must answer 6 questions choosing at least one from each section. In how many ways can 2 from A, 2 from B and 2 from C be chosen? Then also state the count if exactly 3, 2 and 1 are chosen from A, B, C respectively.
questions.answer:
First scheme (2 from A, 2 from B, 2 from C): these choices are independent and all required, so multiply.
   5C2 x 4C2 x 3C2 = 10 x 6 x 3 = 180.

Second scheme (3 from A, 2 from B, 1 from C):
   5C3 x 4C2 x 3C1 = 10 x 6 x 3 = 180.

So each of these specific distributions gives 180 ways. (Each satisfies 'at least one from every section' and totals 6 questions.)
questions.explanation: Multiply section choices: 10 x 6 x 3 = 180 for each scheme.

questions.question: (a) State and verify Pascal's rule nCr + nC(r-1) = (n+1)Cr for n = 6, r = 3. (b) If 15Cr = 15C(r+3), find r. (c) Find the number of triangles formed by 8 points in a plane, of which 3 are collinear.
questions.answer:
(a) Pascal's rule: nCr + nC(r-1) = (n+1)Cr. For n = 6, r = 3: 6C3 + 6C2 = 20 + 15 = 35, and 7C3 = 35. Verified.

(b) 15Cr = 15C(r+3). By the property nCx = nCy, either r = r+3 (impossible) or r + (r+3) = 15, giving 2r + 3 = 15, 2r = 12, r = 6.

(c) With no collinear restriction the number of triangles would be 8C3 = 56. The 3 collinear points cannot form a triangle, and they would have contributed 3C3 = 1 selection. So triangles = 8C3 - 3C3 = 56 - 1 = 55.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.
A small cafe offers a lunch deal where a customer picks one starter, one main course and one drink. There are 3 starters, 4 main courses and 2 drinks available.
(a) State which counting principle applies and why.
(b) How many different lunch deals are possible?
(c) If a new main course is added, how many deals are then possible?
(d) If instead the customer picks only ONE item that is a starter OR a drink, how many choices are there?
questions.answer:
(a) The multiplication principle applies, because the deal is built in successive stages (starter AND main AND drink) that must all be chosen.
(b) 3 x 4 x 2 = 24 different lunch deals.
(c) With 5 main courses: 3 x 5 x 2 = 30 deals.
(d) Picking one item that is a starter OR a drink uses the addition principle (mutually exclusive): 3 + 2 = 5 choices.
questions.explanation: Multiplication for stages (24, then 30); addition for OR (5).

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.
Factorials are the building blocks of counting formulas. Recall n! = n(n-1)...2 x 1, 0! = 1 and n! = n x (n-1)!.
(a) Evaluate 6!.
(b) Simplify 8!/(5! 3!).
(c) Solve n(n-1) = 42 using a factorial relation.
(d) Why is the convention 0! = 1 useful?
questions.answer:
(a) 6! = 720.
(b) 8!/(5!3!) = (8 x 7 x 6)/(3 x 2 x 1) = 336/6 = 56.
(c) n!/(n-2)! = n(n-1) = 42, so n^2 - n - 42 = 0, (n-7)(n+6) = 0, n = 7.
(d) The convention 0! = 1 makes formulas like nPr = n!/(n-r)! and nCn = n!/(n! 0!) give the correct value 1 when r = n, so no special cases are needed.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.
Using the digits 2, 3, 5, 6, 7, 9 with NO repetition, various numbers are formed.
(a) How many 3-digit numbers can be formed?
(b) How many of them are even?
(c) How many are greater than 500 (3-digit)?
(d) How many 6-digit numbers use all the digits?
questions.answer:
There are 6 distinct digits.
(a) 3-digit numbers: 6P3 = 6 x 5 x 4 = 120.
(b) Even means units digit is 2 or 6: 2 choices; the other two places from remaining 5 digits: 5 x 4 = 20. Total = 2 x 20 = 40.
(c) Greater than 500: the hundreds digit must be 5, 6, 7 or 9: 4 choices; remaining two places from the other 5 digits: 5 x 4 = 20. Total = 4 x 20 = 80.
(d) 6-digit numbers using all digits: 6! = 720.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.
The word ENGINEERING is to be rearranged. It has 11 letters: E(3), N(3), G(2), I(2), R(1).
(a) How many distinct arrangements are possible?
(b) How many begin with the letter R?
(c) What is the rule used for repeated letters?
(d) Circular check: in how many ways can 4 distinct letters be seated around a ring?
questions.answer:
(a) Distinct arrangements = 11!/(3! 3! 2! 2!) = 39916800/(6 x 6 x 2 x 2) = 39916800/144 = 277200.
(b) Fix R first; arrange the remaining 10 letters E(3), N(3), G(2), I(2): 10!/(3! 3! 2! 2!) = 3628800/144 = 25200.
(c) When some objects are alike, divide n! by the factorial of the count of each repeated kind: n!/(p! q! ...).
(d) Circular arrangements of 4 distinct letters = (4-1)! = 3! = 6.
questions.explanation: 277200 arrangements; 25200 begin with R; divide by repeats; (4-1)! = 6.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.
A teacher must select students for a quiz. Selection ignores order, so combinations are used, with nCr = n!/(r!(n-r)!).
(a) In how many ways can 3 students be selected from 12?
(b) Relate this to 12P3.
(c) Evaluate 12C9 without heavy computation.
(d) Why is a selection a combination and not a permutation?
questions.answer:
(a) 12C3 = (12 x 11 x 10)/(3 x 2 x 1) = 1320/6 = 220.
(b) 12P3 = 3! x 12C3 = 6 x 220 = 1320 (arranging the 3 selected in order).
(c) 12C9 = 12C(12-9) = 12C3 = 220 by symmetry.
(d) Because only WHO is chosen matters, not the order in which they are picked; different orders of the same students give the same team.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.
A committee of 6 is to be formed from 6 gentlemen and 4 ladies.
(a) In how many ways can it be formed with no restriction?
(b) In how many ways if it must have exactly 2 ladies?
(c) In how many ways with at least 2 ladies?
(d) In how many ways if a particular lady must always be included?
questions.answer:
Total people = 10.
(a) No restriction: 10C6 = 210.
(b) Exactly 2 ladies (and 4 gentlemen): 4C2 x 6C4 = 6 x 15 = 90.
(c) At least 2 ladies = total minus (0 ladies) minus (1 lady). 0 ladies: 6C6 = 1; 1 lady: 4C1 x 6C5 = 4 x 6 = 24. So at least 2 = 210 - 1 - 24 = 185.
(d) One particular lady fixed: choose remaining 5 from the other 9: 9C5 = 126.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.
Combinations have neat properties: nCr = nC(n-r), Pascal's rule nCr + nC(r-1) = (n+1)Cr, and if nCx = nCy then x = y or x + y = n.
(a) Evaluate 18C16 quickly.
(b) If nC5 = nC7, find n.
(c) Verify Pascal's rule for n = 8, r = 4.
(d) State what nC0 + nC1 + ... + nCn equals.
questions.answer:
(a) 18C16 = 18C2 = (18 x 17)/2 = 153.
(b) 5 is not 7, so n = 5 + 7 = 12.
(c) 8C4 + 8C3 = 70 + 56 = 126, and 9C4 = 126. Verified.
(d) It equals 2^n, the total number of subsets of an n-element set.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.
There are 15 points in a plane, of which 6 are collinear (lie on one straight line) and no other three are collinear.
(a) How many straight lines can be drawn?
(b) How many triangles can be formed?
(c) State the correction principle you used.
(d) If none were collinear, how many triangles would there be?
questions.answer:
(a) Lines = 15C2 - 6C2 + 1 = 105 - 15 + 1 = 91 (the 6 collinear points give one line instead of 6C2).
(b) Triangles = 15C3 - 6C3 = 455 - 20 = 435 (subtract triples that are all collinear).
(c) Correction principle: count as if no three were collinear, then remove the degenerate cases caused by the collinear points.
(d) With none collinear: 15C3 = 455 triangles.
questions.explanation: Lines 91; triangles 435; subtract collinear cases; 455 if none collinear.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.
Eight friends attend a dinner.
(a) In how many ways can they sit in a row?
(b) In how many ways can they sit around a round table?
(c) In how many round-table ways if two particular friends sit together?
(d) Why is the round-table count smaller than the row count?
questions.answer:
(a) Row: 8! = 40320.
(b) Round table: (8-1)! = 7! = 5040.
(c) Two friends together at a round table: treat them as one block, giving 7 units around the table: (7-1)! = 6! = 720, times 2! = 2 for the pair's internal order: 720 x 2 = 1440.
(d) The round-table count is smaller because rotations of a circular arrangement are regarded as the same seating, so we fix one person, removing the n rotational duplicates (dividing 8! by 8 gives 7!).
questions.explanation: 40320; 5040; 6! x 2! = 1440; rotations identified reduce the count.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.
The symbol nPr counts ordered arrangements: nPr = n!/(n-r)!.
(a) Evaluate 7P2.
(b) Evaluate 7P0 and 7P7.
(c) If nP2 = 90, find n.
(d) State how nPr and nCr are related.
questions.answer:
(a) 7P2 = 7 x 6 = 42.
(b) 7P0 = 1 and 7P7 = 7! = 5040.
(c) nP2 = n(n-1) = 90, so n^2 - n - 90 = 0, (n-10)(n+9) = 0, n = 10.
(d) They are related by nPr = r! x nCr; permutations are selections that are then arranged.
